subject: Tyska
title: Articles and gender
sourceSummary: The three definite articles der/die/das, the indefinite article, and the plural of nouns.

questions.prompt: How many genders (grammatical genders) do German nouns have?
questions.opener: Unlike Swedish's two (en/ett), German has one more.
questions.explanation: German has three genders: masculine (der), feminine (die), and neuter (das). Gender usually has to be learned together with each word.

questions.prompt: Choose the right article: "___ Haus ist groß." (The house is big.)
questions.explanation: "Haus" (house) is neuter, so the article is "das". "Der" is used for masculine words, "die" for feminine words and plural.

questions.prompt: Choose the right article: "___ Kinder spielen im Garten." (The children are playing in the garden.)
questions.explanation: All plural nouns in German take the article "die", regardless of the word's gender in the singular.

questions.prompt: Choose the right article: "Ich habe ___ Katze." (I have a cat.)
questions.explanation: "Eine" is the indefinite article for feminine ("a/an"). "Ein" is used for masculine/neuter in the nominative.

questions.prompt: What is the plural of "der Tisch" (the table)?
questions.opener: Many masculine words form the plural with -e.
questions.explanation: "Tisch" → "Tische" in the plural, with the article "die" (the plural article for all genders).

questions.prompt: Which definite article (der/die/das) goes with "Mädchen" (girl)? Write just the article.
questions.opener: A classic exception — the word ends in -chen, a diminutive ending that always makes a word neuter.

questions.prompt: Correct the two errors: "Der Katze ist klein und das Hund ist groß."
questions.opener: Check the gender of "Katze" and "Hund" separately.
questions.answer: Die Katze ist klein und der Hund ist groß.
steps: "Der Katze" → "Die Katze". "Katze" (cat) is feminine, so the article should be "die", not "der".
"Das Hund" → "Der Hund". "Hund" (dog) is masculine, so the article should be "der", not "das".
Gender has to be learned word by word — it's rarely possible to guess just from the meaning.

questions.prompt: How does gender, the definite/indefinite articles, and the plural work in German?
questions.opener: The three genders and how the articles follow along.
questions.answer: Gender: der (masculine, e.g. der Mann), die (feminine, e.g. die Frau), das (neuter, e.g. das Kind) — has to be learned with each word, rarely possible to guess. Exception to remember: words ending in -chen or -lein are always "das" (das Mädchen). Indefinite article: ein (masc./neut.), eine (fem.). Plural: always takes the article "die", regardless of the original gender — the word itself is inflected in different ways (-e, -er, -(e)n, or no ending at all).
